questions.q: Why can't a raw classical feature vector like [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] be loaded directly as a quantum state's amplitudes?
options: A valid quantum state's amplitudes must have squared magnitudes summing to exactly 1, which the raw vector does not satisfy -- it must be normalized first in classical code
Quantum circuits can only accept integer values, and some of the entries are not integers
The vector has too few entries to be loaded into any circuit
Classical arrays cannot be read by any software at all
questions.explain: Quantum state amplitudes must satisfy the unit-norm constraint (squared magnitudes summing to 1). A raw feature vector has no such constraint, so classical normalization is a mandatory preprocessing step before amplitude encoding.

questions.q: For the vector [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6], the lesson computes a norm of 13.1529 and a normalized vector whose squared entries sum to 1.000000. How many qubits does amplitude-encoding this 8-value vector require?
options: 3 qubits, since log2(8) = 3
8 qubits, one per value
1 qubit, since all 8 values are packed into a single amplitude
24 qubits, since 8 x 3 = 24
questions.explain: Amplitude encoding indexes n values across log2(n) qubits; for 8 values that's log2(8) = 3 qubits, each holding one amplitude per basis state.

questions.q: What is the key classical preprocessing difference between amplitude encoding and angle encoding?
options: Amplitude encoding mandatorily requires normalizing the vector to unit norm; angle encoding only recommends range-scaling values, since any real number can be used directly as a rotation angle
Both encodings require identical normalization steps
Angle encoding requires normalization to unit norm, while amplitude encoding does not
Neither encoding requires any classical preprocessing
questions.explain: Amplitude encoding's unit-norm constraint is mathematically mandatory because amplitudes must form a valid quantum state. Angle encoding has no such hard constraint -- scaling to a predictable range like [0, 2pi] is recommended for well-behaved rotations, not required by physics.

questions.q: According to the comparison table, why does angle encoding become impractical for a dataset with 1,000 features on near-term hardware?
options: Angle encoding needs one qubit per feature, so 1,000 features would require 1,000 qubits -- far beyond near-term device qubit counts -- while amplitude encoding needs only about log2(1000) ~= 10 qubits
Angle encoding cannot represent more than 8 features under any circumstances
Angle encoding requires more classical preprocessing than amplitude encoding at any scale
1,000 features cannot be represented by any quantum encoding scheme
questions.explain: Angle encoding's one-qubit-per-feature requirement scales linearly and becomes infeasible at 1,000 features, whereas amplitude encoding's logarithmic qubit requirement (~10 qubits) stays feasible, despite its own circuit-depth tradeoff.

questions.q: If classical code skips the normalization step and feeds a raw, un-normalized vector into an amplitude-encoding routine, what does the lesson say typically happens?
options: Most SDKs validate the unit-norm constraint and will fail outright, or in some cases silently rescale in an unintended way -- either way, this is a classical bug, not a quantum hardware issue
The QPU automatically detects and corrects the normalization error at execution time
The circuit runs correctly regardless, since normalization is a cosmetic step with no real effect
The cloud provider bills double for un-normalized submissions
questions.explain: Normalization is a classical-code responsibility. Skipping it produces either an SDK validation failure or unintended silent rescaling -- a bug in your preprocessing code, not a quantum hardware fault.
